summary: This document provides an overview of the Global Soil Partnership (GSP) and the GSOCseq initiative, which aims to map soil organic carbon sequestration potential to support national targets and sustainable soil management.

heading_path: The Global Soil Organic Carbon Sequestration Potential Map (GSOCseq)
passages.text: The Global Soil Organic Carbon Sequestration Potential Map (GSOCseq)

The Global Soil Partnership (GSP) Was established in December 2012 with the main aim of: 1 creating a mechanism to foster strong partnerships and collaboration to place soils on the global agenda; 2 promoting Sustainable Soil Management (SSM); 3 improving the governance of soils.

heading_path: The Global Soil Partnership (GSP) in numbers
passages.text: 10 years of GSP! 8 regional partnerships, over 370 partners worldwide 160 focal points appointed directly by UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization FAO member countries 7 International Networks

GSNmap - Global Soil Nutrient Map.

Following FAO members request, Global Soil Partnership (GSP) has started the GSOCseq initiative to: 1 Set attainable and evidence based national targets for carbon sequestration; 2 Identify areas that have high SOC sequestration for SSM projects 3 Enhance National capacities on sustainable soil management, soil data management, digital soil mapping and modelling; as inputs for NDCs and reporting

heading_path: The GSOCseq approach for reporting CSCs in GHGI
passages.text: It’s important to understand what the GSOCseq approach allows you to report on: CO2 emission/removals in non-waterlogged mineral soils in croplands and grasslands; CO2 emissions/removals in paddy field soils. However, the current GSOCseq has the following limitations: It does not replace the need for ground data as well as the Tier 1 approach; Further parametrization might be needed (e.g. SOC dynamics in Vulcanic soils); It cannot report CO2 emissions/removals for forests; It does not take into account CH4, NO2 emissions.
